posts.title: Airport pickups without the stress
posts.excerpt: Flight delays, meeting points, and wait times — how to make an airport ride effortless.
posts.imageAlt: Car waiting outside an airport terminal
posts.author: Rahul Verma

body.text: Airport rides have more moving parts than a normal trip — flights shift, terminals are large, and parking is tight. A little planning removes almost all of the friction.

items: Add your flight number so the driver can track delays.
Pick a clear meeting point — arrivals curb or a named door.
Allow a few minutes of free wait time for baggage.

body.text: A driver who can see your flight is a driver who is already on the way.

posts.title: What makes a five-star ride
posts.excerpt: Small touches from both sides that turn an ordinary trip into a great one.
posts.imageAlt: Driver smiling in the rear-view mirror
posts.author: Sana Kapoor

body.text: Great rides are rarely about the car. They are about the small, human details that make a stranger feel looked after.

items: A clean cabin and a quick “where would you like the temperature?”
The route confirmed up front, no surprises.
Help with bags, offered not assumed.

posts.title: Riding safely after dark
posts.excerpt: Share your trip, verify the plate, and trust your instincts — a quick safety checklist.
posts.imageAlt: City street at night with car lights
posts.author: Rahul Verma

body.text: Most trips are uneventful, and a few habits keep them that way — especially late at night.

items: Match the car, plate, and driver photo before you get in.
Share your live trip with someone you trust.
Sit in the back and keep a door unlocked.

body.text: If anything feels off, you never owe anyone an explanation for ending a trip early.

posts.title: Planning a multi-stop day
posts.excerpt: Errands, meetings, and a school run in one booking — how multi-stop trips work.
posts.author: Priya Nair

body.text: When your day has several stops, one booking with a planned route beats three separate rides — for cost and for sanity.

items: Add every stop in order before you confirm.
Flag any stop where the driver should wait.
Keep the final destination accurate for the fare estimate.

posts.title: A day in the life of a driver
posts.excerpt: From the morning rush to the late shift — what the road looks like from the front seat.
posts.imageAlt: Driver checking a phone before a shift
posts.author: Sana Kapoor

body.text: Every shift is a string of short stories — a nervous flyer, a first date, a parent running late. Drivers see a city wake up and wind down.
You are never just moving people from A to B; you are part of their day.

posts.title: Understanding your fare
posts.excerpt: Base fare, distance, time, and surge — a plain-English breakdown of what you pay.
posts.imageAlt: Phone showing a trip fare estimate
posts.author: Priya Nair

body.text: A fare is just a few simple parts added together. Knowing them makes every estimate easy to read.

items: Base fare: a fixed amount for starting the trip.
Distance and time: the bulk of most fares.
Surge: a multiplier when demand is high — shown before you confirm.
